title: Taking the music away from big bands
summary: He throws music on the floor in workshops to show the limits of reading from paper.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: I love going around doing this. I mean when I did that one in Chicago, the kids, first of all the teachers always say like — well I always ask them what they want to do. They say, “Well we’d like to work on precision” and things like that. One time with a band from Australia, the precision was mind-boggling. And afterwards he said, “We need to work on precision a little bit.”

I said, “Would you mind if I go in a little different direction?” Because generally when I work with a big band, within ten minutes the stands are away, the music’s away, we just do stuff up, you know, movement and stuff. But the first thing I like to do is like I’ll have the band, the leader will play a couple of pieces so I can hear some of the soloists, you know, hear how they play together. And then I’ll say, “Okay, you guys sound good.” And they do, they work hard and they’re a little nervous but I mean okay. I say, “Now I want you to play the song again but no matter what I do keep playing. If it makes you laugh, try not to laugh, just keep playing. So they start playing and I go around and I’ll go over and take the lead alto player’s music and throw it on the floor, and do that with a few other players and stuff and just like sort of turn the music around. And they’re like hamina-hamina. So then we’ll do it for a while and then we’ll stop. And I’ll say, “Well what was that experience like?” Because they’re married to the music you know.
And I hold up the paper and I say, “What was it like?” I say, “See this paper? See all these black dots and lines? What was invented first, music or paper?”
Especially the drummers, who are like, you know, they can’t get their head out of the paper.
